messages.author: b655697c64cc729d
messages.subject: gdistsamp headaches
parts:
Dear unmarked friends,


I am having troubles with an analysis using gdistsamp. I have bird point count data with 3, 50m distance bands, 2 visits during the breeding season, and a bunch of site-level (habitat) and visit-level (date,time) data. I have attached my data file.

On to the analysis... I had some troubles with very high estimates for phi (and huge SEs) fitting simple (null) models, so I provided starting values and that seemed to fix things. I built up my model until I had all the parameters of interest and associated starting values (see model and output below).


gdistsamp(~Mh+Conifer+V4+V1+Hickory+Oak, ~date+wind+time+temp, ~1, umf, keyfun="hazard", output="abund", K = 15,

starts=c(-0.6047,0.2234,-.2452,-.0745,0.2106,0.1,-.1,0.813,-.903,-1.284,-.181,-.259,4.33,2.01))

Abundance:

            Estimate     SE      z P(>|z|)

(Intercept)  -0.6304 0.2406 -2.620 0.00879

Mh            0.2303 0.1057  2.179 0.02936

Conifer      -0.2065 0.1805 -1.145 0.25239

V4           -0.3579 0.1229 -2.913 0.00358

V1            0.2634 0.0848  3.104 0.00191

Hickory       0.0991 0.0753  1.316 0.18805

Oak          -0.1059 0.1469 -0.721 0.47109

 

Availability:

            Estimate    SE      z P(>|z|)

(Intercept)   0.6238 0.765  0.815  0.4150

date         -0.9627 0.488 -1.972  0.0487

wind         -1.1561 0.522 -2.215  0.0268

time         -0.0884 0.362 -0.244  0.8073

temp         -0.3417 0.371 -0.921  0.3573

 

Detection:

 Estimate     SE    z P(>|z|)

     4.32 0.0871 49.6       0

 

Hazard-rate(scale):

 Estimate    SE   z  P(>|z|)

     1.99 0.231 8.6 7.78e-18

 

AIC: 789.3721


However, my main issue is the GOF test using the full model. Because of slow-running time, I have only attempted up to 20 nsims. However, I get the following error...

Error in optim(starts, nll, method = method, hessian = se, ...) :

  non-finite finite-difference value [13].

 If I try nsims=5 or so, I don’t get errors but it looks like there will be lack of fit (Freeman-Tukey, Pr(t_B > t0) = 0). So my thinking is that I should try finding better explanatory variables, possibly extracting some land cover data? But before doing this, I thought why don’t I simulate some covariate data that fits the abundance data and then see if it passes the GOF test. So that’s what I did, and indeed I still can’t get it to pass the GOF test. Does anybody know a likely cause for this?

I’ve attached my data (umf) in an RData file. The siteCov variable, “lambdacov” is the simulated data.

If anyone has a moment to have a look at this, I would greatly appreciate it.


Thanks

Myles Falconer

Bird Studies Canada

messages.author: 4a15de51da4445ae
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] gdistsamp headaches
parts:
hi Myles,

 With fairly complex models there is a chance of numerical crashes in the optimization and unfortunately our fitting functions are not robust to this, so this can cause problems in the context of simulation studies such as when doing the parametric bootstrapping.  The solution to this is to do the parametric bootstrapping "the long way" -- i.e., do all the simulation, fitting, and summarizing outside of the parboot function.  Another option is to figure out how to rewrite the parboot using the trycatch() function which I've heard people mention before but I'm afraid I don't know how to do that.

 With regard to your second question: if you're simulating data and then fitting the data-generating model then it should pass the  bootstrap goodness-of-fit.... unfortunately I can't take the time right now to search through your simulation code but I suggest starting with the simplest possible model to verify that and then hunt down your probable bug.   

 I wonder if anyone on the unmarked list has tried such a simulation study before and, if so, what was the result?

 In general, there is a need for simulation studies on the power of these tests under various alternatives. It would be a good paper to write if anyone is interested.

regards
andy

messages.author: 247b990d236a7af6
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] gdistsamp headaches
parts:
First, you should follow Andy's advice about starting with a much simpler model.

Second, to expand on what Andy stated about numerical crashes:  Even with all of the resources thrown at PROC MIXED and PROC GLIMMIX in SAS along with mixed models in R using lme4, numerical issues dominate the time I spend dealing with such analyses.  Sometimes standardizing covariates works.  Sometimes better starting values and sometimes tweaking the optimization methods or search parameters works.  (And sometimes recognizing that a model is too complex for the available data is what is required.)  The point is that such functions are near impossible to make "completely" robust to all situations.  And for such models here there is more than one level of generalized linear model!

Third, for such error messages (not only in gdistsamp but others that use optim) using method="Nelder-Mead" and se=FALSE many times makes those errors go away.  (If one is using optim directly, then one uses hessian=FALSE rather than se=FALSE.)

Jim

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] gdistsamp headaches
parts:
Dear all,

just let me throw some code example out for the use of the R function try() to prevent unmarked from crashing when a numerical error occurs. From some Nmix modeling that I did for a very large number of species and scenarios. Hope this is understandable and you can adapt it to your case.

Best regards  --- Marc

      # Fit model with Poisson mixture and do parametric bootstrap GOF
      fmP <- try(pcount(~date+I(date^2) ~forest+elev+I(elev^2), umf, control=list(trace=TRUE,
          REPORT=5, maxit = 300)))
      if (class(fmP) == "try-error") {v<-1} else {
      tmpP <- summary(fmP)
      (pbP <- parboot(fmP, fitstats, nsim=n.boot, report=1))
      stats <- extract.parboot(pbP)
      results[row.number,6:12] <- coef(fmP)
      results[row.number,13:16] <- tmpP$state[,2]
      results[row.number,17:19] <- tmpP$det[,2]
      results[row.number,20] <- fmP@negLogLike
      results[row.number,21] <- fmP@AIC
      results[row.number,22:24] <- stats[,7]
      results[row.number,25:27] <- stats[,6]
      }
